name: Hliðskjálf
powers: From it the sitter can see across all the worlds.
description: Hliðskjálf is the high seat of Odin in Valhöll, from which the All-Father can see across all the worlds and watch everything that happens among gods, men, and giants. The Prose Edda describes it as a throne of far-seeing power, and both Odin and, at times, his wife Frigg use it to scan the cosmos. Sitting in it unbidden was dangerous: the god Freyr once took the seat, was struck by a sight of the giantess Gerðr in the distance, and fell so hopelessly in love that he sent his servant Skírnir to woo her, giving away his own magic sword as payment — the sword whose loss later costs Freyr his life at Ragnarök. The name appears in Skírnismál and throughout the Eddas, and the throne has become the standard image of Odin's all-seeing kingship over the nine worlds.
source: Prose Edda (Gylfaginning); Skírnismál

name: Hringhorni
powers: The greatest of ships, large enough to bear a god's funeral pyre.
description: Hringhorni is the greatest of all ships, the vessel on which the gods laid the body of Baldr the Beautiful after his death by the mistletoe dart. When the gods tried to launch Hringhorni for the funeral, the ship was so heavy that no god or giant could move it, until the giantess Hyrrokkin came riding on a wolf and sent the vessel sliding into the sea with a single shove, the earth shaking with the force. The funeral of Baldr, with the pyre lit on the ship, the ring Draupnir laid upon it, and the dwarf Litr cast into the flames, is one of the most famous scenes in the Prose Edda. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'ring-prowed' or 'ship with a ring-shaped stern'. Hringhorni appears in skaldic references and remains a fixed image in retellings of Baldr's death.
source: Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)

name: Hǫfuð
powers: The sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Edda.
description: Hǫfuð, meaning 'head', is the sword of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Prose Edda. Snorri lists the blade beside Heimdallr's duties as guardian of the gods, and later tradition links the sword to the final battle, in which Heimdallr and Loki are said to slay one another at Ragnarök. Very little else is recorded about the weapon, and no detailed story of its forging or use survives, which makes it one of the more mysterious named swords of the Eddas. The name 'head' is sometimes explained as a kenning-like epithet for a sword, or as a reference to the head that Heimdallr and Loki were said to have fought over. Hǫfuð is nevertheless a fixture in catalogues of Norse mythic weapons, even though its owner's story is told almost entirely through other objects.
source: Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)

name: The Holy Spring
maker: Natural spring, named for a saint
powers: Healing water for the sick who visit on the appointed day.
description: The holy spring (heliga källan), a spring or well that Swedish folk tradition credited with healing. Such springs, often named for a saint, were visited for cures on particular days, usually the saint's feast or a church holiday, and the water was drunk, bathed in, or carried home in flasks for the sick and the cattle. Pilgrims left offerings of coins, linen, or small crosses, often hanging them on a nearby tree, and some springs were said to swell, run warm, or glow before a miracle. When a cure failed, the spring might be slandered as having lost its power. Many Swedish holy springs became local pilgrimage sites that the church later absorbed by blessing them anew, or closed altogether, yet the custom of visiting them survived into the 19th and even the 20th century in parts of the countryside.
source: Swedish holy-spring tradition and place-name studies

name: Hjortspring Boat
description: A slender light war canoe of linden wood, about 18 meters long, dug from a bog on the island of Als, Denmark, in 1921 along with the shields, swords, and spears of a defeated army. Built around 350 BCE, it held perhaps twenty paddlers and was offered up after a battle, likely as a sacrifice of the enemy's arms. Its sewn and lashed plank construction shows a northern boat-building tradition far older than the Viking ships. It is the oldest and finest of the Nordic war boats and rests in the National Museum of Denmark.
source: Bog find, Hjortspring, Als (1921)

name: Perseus' Sickle
powers: Could sever the head of Medusa and shear through stone and serpent.
description: The curved sickle-sword, the harpe, with which Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, given to him by Hermes on his quest. Ancient sources describe it as a sword or sickle that could shear through stone and serpent, and the severed head's gaze still petrified his foes. The deed closes the Medusa episode and arms Athena with the gorgoneion on her aegis. In vase painting Perseus is shown gripping the curved blade while the Gorgon's head falls, a scene that became a standard image of heroic triumph in the Greek world.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; later iconography

name: Hermes’ Sandals
powers: Grants the wearer winged speed and the ability to travel instantly across realms.
description: The talaria, the winged sandals of Hermes, the messenger of the gods in Greek myth, carry the wearer swift as the wind across land and sea and between the realms of mortals and gods; Homer already knows them, and in the Iliad Hermes ties on his 'ambrosial, golden' sandals before his errands. In later art the sandals are always shown with small wings at the ankles, and together with the winged cap and the caduceus they make up the messenger god's badge. They are worn not only by Hermes but by heroes and deities on his errands, and in some accounts give their speed to Perseus in his flight from the Gorgons. The talaria passed into Roman tradition as the attribute of Mercury and were revived in the Renaissance as a symbol of swiftness and eloquence. The winged shoe, with the winged hat, has become the universal shorthand for the courier of the gods.
source: Homeric Hymns

name: Heian Court Fan
powers: Elegant signaling device; used in court dances and ceremonies.
description: The Heian court fan, the hiōgi, is the folding fan of the Japanese court of the 9th to 12th centuries, made of slender strips of cypress wood joined at the base and spread in a fan of pale wood, often painted with seasonal flowers and scenes or inscribed with poems; the folding fan itself is a Japanese invention, and these court fans were among the earliest fans to reach China and Korea. Courtiers of the Heian aristocracy used the fan to conceal the face, to gesture in the dance, to signal discreetly at court, and, in the elaborate etiquette of the age, to express shades of meaning the spoken word could not carry; in the paintings of the Tale of Genji the fan is as much a badge of rank as an accessory. Fans were also carried in the rituals of the court, held before the face in ceremony and in the kagura dance, and a painted fan was a gift that carried the giver's taste and standing. The hiōgi survives in the formal fans of Shinto ritual and in the court dance traditions of Kyoto.
source: Court Artifacts Catalog

name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: The hannya is a Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman transfigured by jealousy, resentment, or obsessive love into a horned, serpent-eyed demon with a gaping, fang-filled mouth and trailing metallic teeth. It is worn in plays such as Dojoji, where a spurned woman becomes a serpent that pursues the monk Anchin into a temple bell, and Aoi no Ue, where the living Rokujo no Miyasudokoro torments her rival through spirit-doctoring. The mask is carved in ascending grades of intensity, from a slightly raised mouth to a fully open jaw with gilded fangs, so a single hannya can move on stage from grief to pure fury. In the folk tradition the finished mask is treated with care because it is thought to retain the dangerous emotional charge it depicts, and carvers historically disposed of flawed examples ritually rather than letting them circulate. The hannya name is also used for the demon itself in the wider yokai lore that grew up around the Noh stage.
source: Noh repertoire (Dojoji; Aoi no Ue)

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: Hagoromo, the feather mantle, is the robe that lets a heavenly maiden, the tennyo, fly between the mortal world and the sky, and it is the central object of one of the most famous Noh plays, Hagoromo, set at Mio Bay. In the play a fisherman named Hakuryo finds a robe of feathers hanging from a pine and refuses to return it until the angel who owns it teaches him the dance of the moon palace, the promise of the robe's return drawing the divine world briefly into the human. The story belongs to the wider family of swan-maiden tales told across Eurasia, in which a supernatural woman loses her flying garment, marries a mortal, and departs when the garment is restored. In Japanese folklore the robe is woven from a thousand feathers and cannot be lifted by any ordinary hand, and a man who hides it may win the maiden's love but loses her when it is found. The play's theme of the boundary between human and divine, and the price of crossing it, has made the hagoromo a staple of Japanese literature and a name given to shrines and dance traditions honouring the heavenly maidens.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of Hou Yi is the weapon of the legendary archer of Chinese myth who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth, leaving a single sun to light the day. Each of the ten suns was the child of the goddess Xihe, and when all ten rose together the world began to burn; Hou Yi, a peerless bowman, felled nine of them with arrows tipped against the sun-birds that drew the solar chariot. In the same cycle of tales his skill earned him the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but his wife Chang'e swallowed it and drifted to the moon, and the archer was left behind. The bow therefore stands for the archetypal marksman and for the human cost of divine power, and Hou Yi is invoked across Chinese literature whenever perfect archery is described. The tale, recorded in Han-era sources and echoed in the poem 'Tianwen', gives the bow a permanent place among the weapons of Chinese mythology.
source: Huainanzi; Shanhaijing tradition

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The heavenly loom is the celestial weaving frame of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who in Chinese myth wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River, the Milky Way. When she married the cowherd Niulang and neglected her weaving, the Jade Emperor or the Queen Mother of the West separated the pair across the river, allowing them to meet only once a year; on the seventh night of the seventh month, magpies form a bridge over the river and the lovers reunite. The tale, first recorded in Han-era poetry, became the origin of the Qixi festival, the Chinese Valentine's day, when girls pray to Zhinü for skill in needlework and for love. The loom is thus the engine of the sky's patterned beauty and the emblem of the craft that the festival celebrates. The same story is told in Korea as Chilseok and in Japan as Tanabata, where the weaving goddess Orihime is remembered with strips of paper hung on bamboo.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources

name: Veracruz Hacha
powers: Emblem of the Mesoamerican ballgame and its rituals.
description: A hacha is a thin, wide stone carving shaped like an axe head but with a deliberately blunt edge, produced in huge numbers by the Classic Veracruz culture of the Gulf lowlands between about 300 and 900 CE. Hachas take the form of human heads, often in profile, and animal faces, carved in fine andesite or basalt with great realism, and the finest examples come from sites such as El Tajin and the Remojadas region. Scholars read them not as working tools but as ballgame emblems, displayed with the great stone yokes and palmas worn by players in the Mesoamerican ballgame; the head-shaped hachas are thought by some to commemorate the severed heads of sacrificed players. Their varied faces make them a key record of Classic Veracruz religious imagery, linking the ballgame to sun worship and sacrifice. Hundreds survive in museums, prized as one of the finest portrait traditions of ancient Mexico.
source: Archaeological corpus of Classic Veracruz carvings

name: Huipil
material: Cotton woven on a backstrap loom
powers: Carries the sacred patterns of the wearer's town and lineage.
description: The huipil is the loose cotton blouse woven and embroidered by Maya women of highland Guatemala, each town preserving its own colours, patterns and motifs that encode lineage, landscape and the sacred order. It is made on the backstrap loom, a pre-Columbian technology in which the weaver controls the tension with her own body, and the knowledge of patterns passes from mother to daughter. Motifs such as mountains, quetzal birds, suns and ancestors link the garment to Maya cosmology, and Ix Chel, the goddess of the moon and of weaving, is said to have taught the craft. Spanish colonial authorities taxed the garment and at times tried to suppress it, yet it survived and became a powerful emblem of Maya identity. Today huipiles are worn daily and at festivals across the highlands, and their woven patterns are studied by anthropologists as a living textile code.
source: Colonial records and living Maya weaving tradition

name: Hex Sign
material: Painted wooden or tin barn disk
powers: Wards off harm and invites luck on the barn.
description: Hex signs are the painted circles and eight-point stars fixed to Pennsylvania Dutch barns from the 18th century onward, their bright patterns of tulips, hearts, distelfinks and stars drawn from the folk art and fraktur of German-speaking settlers. The word 'hex' comes from the German Hexe, 'witch', and many outsiders came to believe the signs were charms to ward off witchcraft, bad luck and fire; in local Pennsylvania German, 'hex' can also mean 'spell'. Scholars argue that the protective meanings were largely a popular invention layered over decoration, though some symbols such as stars clearly carried good-luck associations. Painted by barn artists on the large gable-end 'banks' of Swiss-German barns, the signs became a regional icon of southeastern Pennsylvania. Today hex signs are a celebrated folk art, reproduced on houses, businesses and souvenirs across Berks County.
source: Pennsylvania Dutch folk art and regional studies

name: Haint Blue Paint
material: Pale blue-green paint, traditionally with indigo or lime
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Keeps haints, the wandering spirits, from entering the house.
description: Haint blue is the pale blue-green paint used on porch ceilings, doors and window frames of Gullah homes in the Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia, said to keep haints, the restless spirits of the dead, from entering the house. Water is traditionally the veil between the living and the dead, and the blue is read as the colour of water that haints cannot cross; the eerie 'boo hag' who slips in through keyholes is among the beings the colour is meant to repel. Some writers also trace the hue to practical roots, noting that the lime-based blue paint helped repel insects and resist damp, and that indigo dye was a staple of Lowcountry plantations. The custom has spread far beyond the Sea Islands into a popular Southern decorative style, with paint companies selling shades called haint blue. For the Gullah, the paint remains a visible sign of a protective, deeply held worldview.
source: Gullah oral tradition and regional studies

name: Harpoon
material: Wood shaft with toggle-head of bone or ivory
powers: Strikes the seal and holds it even as the line plays out.
description: The harpoon of the Inuit is the throwing weapon perfected for the open sea, a wooden shaft fitted with a detachable head of bone or ivory that buries itself in the seal's hide and toggles, turning beneath the skin so the animal cannot tear free as the line plays out. The hunter cast from the kayak, holding the line so that the wounded seal could be hauled in as it tired, and the same principle was scaled up with heavier heads and floats for walrus and whales. The design is one of the great achievements of Arctic engineering, refined over millennia of open-water hunting, and it was among the tools that European whalers and explorers adopted and copied. In the belief of the Inuit, the success of the hunt was bound to the goodwill of the sea mother Sedna, who released the animals to a hunter who honored her; a harpoon cast without that favor was said to come back empty. The toggle-head harpoon remains a symbol of the Arctic hunter's skill and restraint.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Herati Carpet
description: The herati carpet is a hand-knotted wool carpet of the Herat region of western Afghanistan, woven with repeating medallion, star and floral patterns that have been exported from the city for centuries. The trade flourished under the Timurid court, when Herat was a centre of craft and patronage, and the rug's patterns are still carried by weaving families who pass the designs from one generation to the next. The name herati is also attached in the rug trade to a pattern with a central diamond, hooked leaves and corner motifs, and the same terms cause lasting confusion with the rugs of Heriz in north-west Iran, which are distinct carpets from a different region. Afghan herati rugs are made of wool on cotton warps, often with the reds and blues of madder and indigo dyes, and are laid as household and prayer carpets.
source: Carpet history of the Herat weaving region

name: Hei Tiki
description: The hei tiki is the carved greenstone pendant worn at the neck by the Maori, representing a human figure with the head tilted to one side, often with the tongue pointing from the mouth. It is made from pounamu, the nephrite jade of the South Island, and carved with stone drills and abrasive cords in the time before metal tools. The hei tiki is a taonga passed down within families, worn by men and women, and the older a pendant is, the more it is valued, for each one is believed to carry the presence and mana of the ancestors who wore it before. New pendants are given as gifts to mark births, weddings and farewells, and the form appears in Maori tradition in the story of the origin of the tiki, which tells how the first human figure was shaped.
maker: Māori carvers of the greenstone trade routes
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Māori adornment and taonga

name: Hāngi (Māori Earth Oven)
description: Traditional earth oven of the Māori, in which stones that can withstand great heat — usually river and greywacke stones rather than beach rocks, which can shatter — are heated in a shallow pit until white-hot. Food is laid on the stones in woven baskets, covered with leaves and cloth, and sealed with earth so that the meal steams slowly over several hours. The hāngi has cooked for hui (gatherings), tangihanga (funerals), Waitangi Day and Christmas for generations, and while modern cooks often heat the stones with gas, the principle and the shared meal remain the heart of Māori hospitality.
source: Ethnographic records of Māori cooking traditions

name: Hawaiian Feather Cloak (ʻAhuʻula)
description: Royal cloak of the Hawaiian chiefs, built on a netted base of olonā fibre and covered with hundreds of thousands of small feathers tied in bundles by a technique called kahekahe. Yellow feathers were taken from the ʻōʻō and mamo — birds whose feathers were pulled by the tens of thousands, contributing to their extinction — and red from the ʻiʻiwi and ʻapapane; Kamehameha I's great cloak is said to contain some 450,000 yellow mamo feathers. The ʻahuʻula was the mark of the highest aliʻi, worn in war and ceremony as a living symbol of chiefly mana and passed down as the supreme heirloom of the kingdom, and surviving examples are counted among the treasures of world museums.
maker: Hawaiian feather workers of the chiefly courts
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Hawaiian regalia

name: Hawaiian Pahu (Drum)
description: Standing drum of the Hawaiian islands, carved from a single log of coconut or breadfruit wood and headed with sharkskin or stingray skin stretched and braced with cords. Two kinds are known: the pahu hula, struck with the hands to accompany the hula and chant, and the larger pahu heiau, the sacred temple drum beaten in the heiau to summon the gods and mark the rites of the priests. The drum stands upright and is played with open palms or heel and fingertips, and in the temple it was considered so sacred that only certain priests might sound it, its rhythms regarded as a channel of divine mana.
material: coconut or breadfruit wood, sharkskin, fibre cord
source: Ethnomusicological studies of Hawaiian music

name: Hawaiian Kapa (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of the Hawaiian islands, beaten by women from the inner bark of the wauke, the paper mulberry, on a stone anvil with grooved wooden beaters, and joined and felted into wide sheets. The cloth was printed by stamping with carved bamboo tubes and blocks and with leaves and water-stamped patterns, in colours drawn from earth, charcoal and plants, and the designs were named and passed down within families. Kapa served as clothing, bedding, bandages and swaddling, and in ritual it wrapped the dead and clothed the altars, so that the finest pieces carried the mana of the maker and the household.
source: Ethnographic records of Hawaiian material culture
